# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Background and rationale

Contemporary metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) have markedly improved the outcomes of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), yet the permanent presence of a metallic frame and durable polymer has been linked to persistent local inflammation, impaired vasomotion, neoatherosclerosis, and a small but ongoing annual risk of late and very late stent failure [16]. In patients with coronary artery disease who receive metallic drug-eluting coronary stents, adverse events such as late target-lesion failure may be related in part to the persistent presence of the metallic stent frame in the coronary-vessel wall; bioresorbable vascular scaffolds have been developed to attempt to improve long-term outcomes. The conceptual appeal was elegant: a device that provides drug delivery and mechanical support during the period of vessel healing, then disappears, restoring vasomotor function and removing the long-term nidus for adverse events.

## The Absorb era: pivotal randomised trials

The everolimus-eluting Absorb bioresorbable vascular scaffold (BVS) became the most extensively studied device. The Absorb BVS provides early drug delivery and mechanical support similar to those of metallic drug-eluting stents, followed by complete resorption in approximately 3 years with recovery of vascular structure and function. In the pivotal US trial, 2008 patients with stable or unstable angina were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive an everolimus-eluting bioresorbable vascular (Absorb) scaffold or an everolimus-eluting cobalt-chromium (Xience) stent [7]. Treatment with the bioresorbable scaffold was within the prespecified margin for noninferiority with respect to target-lesion failure at 1 year. Similar one-year noninferiority was reported in the ABSORB II, ABSORB Japan, and ABSORB China programmes, and a pooled patient-level meta-analysis confirmed comparable early outcomes [8,9,10].

However, the longer-term signal was unfavourable. The ABSORB II 3-year trial was negative for both co-primary endpoints: it did not meet its co-primary endpoints of superior vasomotor reactivity and non-inferior late luminal loss, and a higher rate of device-oriented composite endpoint due to target vessel myocardial infarction was observed in the Absorb group [11]. In ABSORB III, between 1 and 3 years and cumulative to 3 years, adverse event rates—particularly target vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis—were increased after BVS [12]. Reassuringly, longer follow-up suggested that the excess risk was time-limited: cumulative 5-year adverse event rates were increased after BVS compared with everolimus-eluting stents, but the period of excess risk for BVS ended at 3 years, coincident with complete scaffold resorption [13].

## Scaffold thrombosis: the defining safety concern

The principal limitation of first-generation BVS was an increased risk of scaffold thrombosis. An early meta-analysis of randomised trials found that among 2309 patients with the bioresorbable device, the rate of definite or probable thrombosis was 1.3% compared with 0.5% in those who received a Xience stent [14]. A pooled analysis quantified the excess risk across time: BVS as compared with EES was associated with higher risk for very late scaffold thrombosis between 1 and 2 years and stent/scaffold thrombosis through 2 years [15]. A comprehensive registry-and-trial meta-analysis estimated that the overall rate of definite or probable scaffold thrombosis was 1.8%, with a rate of very late thrombosis of 1.0% [16]. A large network meta-analysis subsequently confirmed that patients treated with the Absorb BVS had a significantly higher risk of definite or probable scaffold thrombosis than those treated with metallic DES, with the risk of very late thrombosis highest among comparators [17]. Contributing mechanisms include thick struts, late strut discontinuity, malapposition, and suboptimal implantation technique.

The independent AIDA all-comers trial echoed these findings. There was no significant difference between the study groups in the primary outcome of target-vessel failure, but treatment with the bioresorbable scaffold was associated with a significantly higher incidence of overall and very late device thrombosis than the metallic stent through 2 years [18].

## Optimised technique: ABSORB IV and COMPARE-ABSORB

Because suboptimal sizing and deployment were implicated, ABSORB IV employed an improved "PSP" implantation technique (predilatation, appropriate sizing, postdilatation) with blinded outcome adjudication. The primary endpoint occurred in 7.8% of patients who received Absorb and in 6.4% of patients who received Xience, achieving the limit for non-inferiority [19]. Even so, the COMPARE-ABSORB trial, which mandated optimal implantation, demonstrated no clinical advantage for the scaffold [20], and 5-year ABSORB IV data showed mixed long-term outcomes [21]. A meta-analysis of randomised trials concluded that scaffold use was associated with greater risk of both target-lesion failure and thrombosis [22], and the original device was ultimately withdrawn from the market.

## Beyond Absorb: magnesium and thinner-strut scaffolds

Attention turned to alternative platforms. The sirolimus-eluting magnesium-based Magmaris scaffold was evaluated in BIOSOLVE-II: at 6 months the in-segment late lumen loss was 0.27 ± 0.37 mm [23], with sustained 12-month performance [24]. In ST-elevation myocardial infarction, the MAGSTEMI randomised trial compared a magnesium scaffold against a sirolimus-eluting stent [25], while the ISAR-Absorb MI trial assessed the Absorb BVS against an everolimus-eluting stent in infarct patients [26]. Newer thin-strut polymeric devices are emerging: the FUTURE-I first-in-man study reported favourable early imaging outcomes for the thinner-strut Firesorb scaffold [27], and the randomised FUTURE-II trial demonstrated that the 1-year rate of target lesion failure was numerically lower for the Firesorb group versus Xience (0.9% vs 1.9%) [28]. The self-expanding DESolve novolimus-eluting scaffold represents a further design iteration [29].

## Current status and future directions

The collective evidence prompted clear guidance: only the Absorb scaffold had published randomised data, which showed inferior outcomes to conventional DES at 2-3 years, and for this reason BRS should not be preferred to conventional DES in clinical practice [30]. The first generation thus failed to fulfil its promise, undone chiefly by thick struts and thrombosis. Nonetheless, the underlying rationale remains sound, and thinner-strut, faster-resorbing, better-deliverable next-generation devices—coupled with mandatory intravascular imaging guidance and optimised technique—may yet allow bioresorbable technology to find a defined clinical niche.
